column2: Executive summary

Every dollar this organization earns, and nearly every dollar it spends, passes through one place: the daily schedule. Referrals come in, clinicians go out, and visit volume, margin, and patient outcomes are all set by how well those two sides are matched each day. Scheduling is not a back-office function. It is the operating core of the business, and today we run it largely blind.

Finance has asked a fair question: why build a product when we could put each branch on a spreadsheet and have an AI optimize it every morning? The honest answer is that the spreadsheet is not the hard part. The hard part is that the inputs change hour by hour, the constraints are tangled together, and no one has ever measured how much capacity we actually have. A model can only optimize the numbers you give it, and today those numbers do not exist in any reliable form.

So we are not proposing to solve scheduling. No one has. We are proposing to solve the part that pays for itself first: turning capacity into a measured number, branch by branch, day by day, for the first time. That instrument shows us where we are leaving visits and revenue on the table, and it sharpens every month as it accumulates history that cannot be recreated after the fact. The same instrument extends directly to hospice, where the scheduling problem is the same shape. We are asking to fund a measurement asset that compounds, not a one-time fix.
The schedule is the entire business, in one place
Trace any patient and every referral dollar follows the same path. The schedule is the valve the whole business flows through:
Referral (potential)   ->   Capacity decision (the hinge)   ->   Schedule (the plan)   ->   Visit (the only revenue-producing event)   ->   Outcome & revenue (what finance measures)

Everything upstream of the capacity decision (intake volume, referral relationships, sales) is only potential. Everything downstream (clinical outcomes, revenue, quality scores, patient experience, clinician retention) is gated by whether the right clinician reaches the right home at the right time. The constraint on this business is rarely demand. It is the schedule's ability to convert demand into delivered care.
Why the schedule fights back every hour
A home visit is not one constraint, it is a dozen that must all be true at once, and several of them fight each other. For a single visit to be correct, all of the following have to reconcile:

Discipline and licensure match (SN, PT, OT, ST, MSW, HHA, none of which substitute for one another)  -  geography and drive time  -  the clinician's finite daily capacity and caseload  -  the physician-ordered visit frequency and the LUPA payment threshold  -  active orders and authorization windows  -  patient acuity and clinical timing (start of care within 48 hours, wound-care cadence, medication timing)  -  caregiver presence in the home  -  continuity of care (the same clinician)  -  clinician PTO, same-day call-outs, and turnover  -  patient preference and availability

These constraints conflict. Continuity fights geography. Productivity fights acuity.  And it is dynamic, not static: a single 7 a.m. nurse call-out can invalidate six visits, each with its own clock and financial exposure, and the schedule that was optimal at 8 a.m. is stale by 9. This is a combinatorial problem that reshuffles itself all day long.
Taking the spreadsheet-and-AI idea seriously, then retiring it

The instinct that AI belongs in this problem is correct, and our product uses it. The disagreement is narrower than it looks: it is not AI or no AI, it is an AI running loose on a disposable sheet versus an AI engineered into a system that remembers, measures, and enforces the rules. A daily spreadsheet fails on five counts:
The daily-sheet approach assumes...
A fresh sheet each morning is fine.
column6: It has amnesia. With no history it cannot trend, forecast, or prove ROI, and it cannot catch a branch quietly degrading. For finance this is fatal: you cannot defend a spend that keeps no record of improvement.

column6: The real constraints (licensure, authorizations, LUPA thresholds, drive time, caregiver availability, continuity) live across the EMR, referral, HR/credentialing, payroll, and routing systems. A hand-built sheet omits them or requires massive daily re-keying across ~80 branches. Fed blanks, an optimizer returns a clean-looking answer that is wrong.

column2: It produces the schedule, which is the goal.
column6: The value is not the schedule, it is the measurement. A capacity system answers 'can we take this referral' with a number. A disposable sheet produces output, not knowledge, and throws the knowledge away every night.

column6: Scheduling clinical visits is a high-harm process. With no constraint enforcement, no audit trail, and no accountability, a wrong assignment is a patient-safety and compliance event, not a cosmetic bug.

column6: That does not scale to a national network, does not survive turnover, creates no shared source of truth, and leaves nothing for auditors or surveyors. And it never compounds: next quarter is exactly as blind as this one.

column2: What we are deliberately not trying to solve

If capacity and scheduling were a solvable software problem it would already be solved, because the whole industry has every incentive and has been trying for two decades. Every major platform ships a scheduling module, and every agency running one still staffs teams of human schedulers who override it daily. That is the tell. So the responsible posture, and the one that should earn credibility, is that we are not trying to solve the whole thing through automations.  Where does the human need to remain in the loop and to what degree at each stage of the process and decision node?

The MVP does not build the schedule. It gives schedulers and leaders visibility they have never had: it surfaces real capacity before intake accepts a referral it cannot staff, flags LUPA risk while there is still time to act, and ranks the day's disruption by clinical and financial risk when a call-out hits. The full product moves from surfacing information to proposing options a scheduler accepts or overrides, and forecasting shortfalls days ahead. Fully autonomous scheduling across these conflicting, volatile constraints stays genuinely hard, and any vendor promising it should be treated with suspicion. Being explicit about that boundary is the reason to believe the rest.
For the first time, capacity becomes a number we can see

Ask any branch 'can you take another patient right now' and you get an answer, but never a number behind it. Capacity today is a gut-feel judgment held in a scheduler's head: real expertise, but invisible, unrecorded, and impossible to audit, compare, or improve. Two identical branches can give opposite answers on the same day and no one can say which is right. When a branch turns down a referral, there is usually no record it happened.

The first job of this product is not to optimize anything. It is to make capacity measurable and observable, and to convert the branch director's mental model into a quantified, defensible figure that updates as reality changes. You cannot manage, price, or improve what you cannot measure. Once capacity is a measured number it becomes an input to hiring, to referral acceptance, to territory design, and eventually to payer negotiations, every one of which is made today without it.

The same instrument extends to hospice

Strip away the labels and home health and home-based hospice solve one problem: the right clinician, with the right skills, in the right home, at the right time, under real constraints. The matching engine does not care whether the visit is a skilled-nursing visit or a hospice routine-home-care visit. What changes is the ruleset on top, and that is configuration, not a rebuild. Rosters, licensure, geography, availability, caseloads, visit-frequency tracking and the capacity measurement itself all transfer directly.

Four hospice mechanics need rules added, not new products: interdisciplinary group (IDG) scheduling on the required 15-day plan-of-care cycle; RN case-manager caseloads and the recertification face-to-face; per-diem reimbursement by level of care (routine, continuous, general inpatient, respite), where the scheduling decision is directly a margin decision; and 24/7 on-call and continuous-care staffing. The stakes are higher here: a late or missed visit near end of life becomes a permanent, publicly reported CAHPS Hospice verdict on the branch. Buying the engine once and pointing it at both lines does not double the cost; it roughly doubles the return, on the line where getting it wrong hurts most.
Why it compounds, and the cost of waiting

This is not a one-time optimizer. Every cycle it runs, it captures data the company has never systematically had: true availability, true visit completion, true drive times, true demand arrivals, and every referral taken or turned down. That record is the asset. Each layer of it unlocks the next, harder problem: measure capacity, then forecast demand, then staff proactively to territory, then predict call-outs, then load-balance across branches. None of it is buildable on day one, because each step needs the data the prior step produced. The product manufactures the raw material for its own next version.
